15190:
Stertorous is an adjective that describes a very specific kind of breathing — breathing that is noisy, heavy, and makes a deep snoring or rattling sound. Think of the loud, rumbling, almost gurgling sound that comes from someone's throat when they are in a very deep, heavy sleep, or when they are unconscious. That is the sound "stertorous" captures.

It is not just any loud breathing. It points to a particular quality of sound — low, coarse, and rasping, as if air is being forced through a partly blocked or relaxed throat with great effort.

Imagine someone who has fallen into such a deep, heavy sleep that their jaw goes slack, their throat muscles relax completely, and every breath they draw produces a loud, grinding, snore-like sound. Or imagine a person who has fainted, or is in a coma — breathing slowly but with each breath making a harsh, rattling noise in their throat. That is stertorous breathing.

The word almost always points to breathing that signals reduced consciousness — deep sleep, unconsciousness, a medical emergency, or the final stages of life.
Where and How It Is Used

Stertorous is used in two main worlds:

1. Medical and clinical settings
Doctors and nurses use this word to describe a patient's breathing when it becomes worryingly noisy and labored. Stertorous breathing is a recognized medical sign — it can indicate a stroke, a severe brain injury, a drug overdose, or very deep unconsciousness. When a doctor writes that a patient's breathing is stertorous, it is a warning flag that the person's airway or nervous system is under serious stress.

A related phenomenon you may have heard of is the "death rattle" — the rasping, gurgling sound that sometimes occurs in a person's final hours of life. This is a form of stertorous breathing.

2. Literary and descriptive writing
Writers — especially older, classic writers — use "stertorous" to paint a vivid auditory picture of a character who is deeply drunk, unconscious, exhausted, or gravely ill. It is a powerful, precise word that tells you in one stroke that someone is out — not lightly dozing, but profoundly gone from the waking world.

• The old man lay in the hospital bed, his stertorous breathing the only sound in the room.
  • After drinking heavily, he collapsed on the sofa and fell into a stertorous sleep.
  • The paramedics noted the patient's stertorous respirations and immediately prepared to secure his airway.
  • From behind the closed door came the stertorous snoring of her exhausted father.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Stertorous" carries a somewhat heavy, grim, and clinical tone. It is not a neutral or gentle word. When you call someone's breathing stertorous, you are not just saying they snore — you are suggesting something more serious, more alarming. It implies vulnerability, helplessness, and often danger. A person breathing stertorously is not in control; they are deeply under, and their body is working hard just to keep air moving.

Because of this weight, the word is rarely used in casual, everyday conversation. You will find it most in medical reports, serious literary fiction, or precise descriptive writing where the author wants to convey the gravity of someone's condition.

It is worth being clear about what stertorous does not describe:

  • It does not describe fast or panicked breathing (that would be hyperventilation or rapid breathing).
  • It does not describe the high-pitched whistling sound of asthma or a blocked windpipe (that is called wheezing).
  • It does not simply mean loud in a general sense — there is a specific snoring or rattling quality to it.
  • Do not confuse it with stentorian, which sounds similar but means something entirely different: a very powerful, booming voice (like a general addressing troops). Stentorian is about a strong, commanding voice; stertorous is about labored, unconscious-sounding breathing.

If you had to define it in one sentence: Stertorous describes breathing that is noisy, coarse, and produces a heavy snoring or rattling sound — the kind heard in someone who is deeply unconscious, gravely ill, or in an extremely deep sleep.
15191: A stethoscope is a medical instrument that doctors, nurses, and other healthcare professionals use to listen to sounds happening inside your body — particularly sounds made by your heart, lungs, and stomach — without cutting you open or using any technology that requires electricity.

Your body is constantly making sounds. Your heart beats, your lungs fill with air and push it out, your blood rushes through vessels, and your stomach gurgles. Most of these sounds are too faint to hear with the naked ear from a distance. A stethoscope solves this by collecting those sounds right at the skin's surface and channeling them directly into the examiner's ears, making them clear enough to analyze.

Think of it like pressing a glass against a wall to hear a conversation on the other side — except far more precise and purpose-built for the human body.

A stethoscope has three main parts:

1. The chest piece — This is the end that touches your body. It has two sides:

  • A flat, circular disc called the diaphragm (the larger side). This picks up higher-pitched sounds, like normal breath sounds and most heart sounds.
  • A small, bowl-shaped cup called the bell (the smaller, recessed side). This picks up lower-pitched sounds, like certain abnormal heart murmurs and some vascular sounds.

The examiner presses the appropriate side against your skin depending on what they're listening for.

2. The tubing — Flexible rubber or plastic tubes carry the sound from the chest piece upward. Many stethoscopes have two tubes running side by side (or molded together), one for each ear, to deliver sound to both ears simultaneously.

3. The earpieces (ear tips) — Soft, angled tips that fit snugly into the examiner's ear canals. The angle is intentional — they tilt slightly forward to follow the natural direction of the ear canal, ensuring a good seal so outside noise doesn't interfere.

A stethoscope works on a surprisingly simple physical principle: sound is vibration, and vibration travels.

When your heart beats or your lungs move air, they cause the skin and tissue above them to vibrate very slightly. When the chest piece is pressed against that skin, those vibrations travel into the chest piece. The diaphragm (or bell) captures and amplifies the vibration. That vibration then travels as a sound wave through the closed tubing system — which acts like a sealed acoustic channel — and arrives at the examiner's ears.

Because the tube is closed and sealed, the sound doesn't leak out or mix with room noise. It's delivered cleanly and directly.

This is called acoustic transmission — no batteries, no electronics (in a standard stethoscope), just physics. Sound energy travels from your body, through a sealed tube, into ears.

The stethoscope is most famously used to listen to the heart and lungs, but its uses are broader:

Heart:

  • The rhythm (is it beating regularly or irregularly?)
  • The rate (how fast or slow?)
  • Heart sounds — a healthy heart makes a classic "lub-dub" sound from the closing of its valves. Any extra sounds, clicks, or whooshing noises (called murmurs) can signal a leaky or narrowed valve or other problems.

Lungs:

  • Normal breathing produces a soft, breezy sound. Abnormal sounds reveal problems:
    • Crackles (a crackling or popping sound) can suggest fluid in the lungs, like in pneumonia or heart failure.
    • Wheezes (a high-pitched whistling) suggest narrowed airways, like in asthma.
    • Absent breath sounds on one side could mean a collapsed lung.

Abdomen (stomach and intestines):

  • The gut makes gurgling sounds as it moves food along. A doctor listens to check if the bowel is active or unusually quiet (which can signal a blockage or other issue).

Blood vessels:

  • Doctors can listen over large arteries (like the carotid in the neck or the aorta in the abdomen) for abnormal sounds called bruits (a whooshing or blowing noise), which can indicate turbulent blood flow from a narrowing or blockage.

Blood pressure:

  • When a doctor takes your blood pressure using an inflatable cuff on your arm, they place the stethoscope over the artery at your elbow. They listen for specific sounds (called Korotkoff sounds) that appear and disappear as the cuff is deflated. The pressures at which those sounds start and stop give the two numbers of your blood pressure reading.

While the basic acoustic stethoscope described above is by far the most common, there are a few variations worth knowing:

  • Acoustic stethoscope — The classic, non-electronic version described throughout this explanation. Used by the vast majority of healthcare workers daily.
  • Electronic stethoscope — Converts sound vibrations into an electrical signal, amplifies it electronically, and then converts it back to sound. Useful for doctors who are hard of hearing, or for listening in noisy environments. Some can even record heart sounds or transmit them wirelessly.
  • Fetal stethoscope (Pinard horn) — A simple, trumpet-shaped device used to listen to a baby's heartbeat in the womb. It's placed on the mother's abdomen.
  • Doppler stethoscope — Uses ultrasound waves instead of acoustic sound to detect blood flow. Often used in obstetrics to hear a fetal heartbeat early in pregnancy.

The stethoscope is one of the most iconic symbols of medicine for good reason. It has been a cornerstone of physical examination for nearly two centuries and remains essential today despite the existence of sophisticated imaging technology like MRI and ultrasound. It is cheap, portable, instant, and non-invasive. A skilled clinician can detect serious conditions — a failing heart valve, pneumonia, an asthma attack, a blocked artery — in seconds, simply by listening.

It also plays an important role in the doctor-patient relationship. The act of a doctor placing a stethoscope on a patient's chest is an intimate, attentive gesture — a signal that the doctor is carefully listening to what the body is saying.

In short: a stethoscope is the instrument that lets a trained human ear hear the quiet, hidden language of a living body.
15192:
A stew is a dish made by cooking ingredients — most often pieces of meat, vegetables, or both — slowly in a relatively small amount of liquid, usually water, broth, or stock. The cooking happens over gentle, low heat for a long time, often one to three hours.

The result is a thick, rich, hearty dish. Unlike soup — which is mostly liquid with ingredients floating in it — a stew has very little liquid relative to its solid ingredients. That liquid is thick and almost sauce-like, not thin and watery. The pieces of meat and vegetables in a stew are chunky, not finely chopped, and they become very soft and tender by the time the stew is done. Because everything simmers together slowly in one pot, the flavors blend deeply over time. The meat releases its juices into the liquid, the vegetables absorb those flavors, and the whole thing becomes something richer and more complex than the sum of its parts.

Common examples include beef stew (chunks of beef with carrots, potatoes, and onions in a deep brown broth), Irish stew (lamb with potatoes and onions), fish stew (chunks of fish in a seasoned broth), and vegetable stew (entirely plant-based).
Stew vs. soup — the key distinction

Since this confusion is very common, it is worth addressing clearly. The difference lies in the ratio of liquid to solid ingredients, and in the thickness of that liquid. Soup is mostly liquid — you can drink it straight from a bowl. A stew is mostly solid, with just enough thick liquid to bind everything together and coat it richly. If you tipped a bowl of soup sideways, most of it would pour out easily. If you tipped a bowl of stew, it would move reluctantly, almost like one heavy mass. A stew is also generally more filling and satisfying than a soup.

In informal English, "a stew" can also describe a state of anxiety, worry, or mental agitation. This meaning almost always appears in the fixed phrase "in a stew."

If someone is in a stew, they are feeling unsettled, stressed, or flustered about something — unable to calm down or think clearly. It is not mild worry; it is a kind of heated, restless inner disturbance. The visual parallel is quite apt: just as food in a pot of stew bubbles and simmers restlessly under heat, a person in a stew is mentally bubbling — worked up and unable to settle.

You might say: "She was in a stew about her exam results." Or: "Don't get yourself in a stew — it'll be fine." Or: "He's been in a stew all day, pacing around the office."
Historical meanings — rare, but good to know

In older English, "stew" carried two additional meanings you are unlikely to encounter in everyday modern life, but may come across in historical texts or older literature.

The first is a man-made pond or tank used to keep live fish — usually trout or carp — until they were needed for eating. These were common in medieval Europe, especially near monasteries and large estates. If you ever read a medieval or Renaissance text and see "stew" referring to water or fish, this is what it means.

The second, usually seen in the plural form "the stews," referred to a brothel or a neighborhood known for prostitution. This usage appears in Shakespeare and other writers from roughly the 16th to 18th centuries and is entirely obsolete in modern English.

In short: In everyday life, "stew" as a noun almost always means one of two things — the slow-cooked, thick, hearty dish of meat and vegetables, or the informal state of being anxious and worked up. The first is by far the more common. The second is useful to recognize when reading or listening to informal English.
15193: The verb stew has two lives — one in the kitchen, and one in the mind. Both share the same underlying feeling: something sitting in heat, slowly, for a long time.

To stew food means to cook it slowly in liquid — water, broth, sauce, or juice — over low heat for a long period of time.

This is not the same as boiling (which is fast and violent) or frying (which uses fat, not liquid). Stewing is a gentle, patient, slow process. The food is either fully or mostly submerged in liquid, and everything cooks together quietly over a long time.

The result? The food becomes very soft and tender, and the liquid around it turns thick, rich, and full of flavour.

Examples:

  • She stewed the beef for three hours until it fell apart.
  • He stewed the apples with sugar and cinnamon.
  • The tomatoes were stewed until they turned into a thick sauce.

You can stew meat (beef, lamb, chicken), vegetables, and even fruits like prunes or pears. The key idea is always: slow + liquid + low heat + long time.
Meaning 2: To Worry or Brood (The Figurative Sense)

This is where the word gets really interesting. When a person stews, it means they are worrying about something, brooding over it, or feeling anxious or upset — but they are doing it silently and repeatedly, without taking action.

Think about how food stews: it sits in heat, bubbling quietly, going nowhere, for a long, long time. Now imagine a person doing the same thing — but instead of liquid and heat, they are sitting inside their own worry or anger, going nowhere, for a long time. That is what it means for a person to stew.

It is not a quick flash of anger or a short moment of worry. It is prolonged, slow, internal, and often unproductive. The person is trapped in their own thoughts, turning the same problem over and over, usually without resolving anything.

Examples:

  • He stewed over the argument all night instead of sleeping.
  • She made a mistake at work and spent the whole weekend stewing about it.
  • Don't just stew — talk to her and fix it!
  • He sat in the corner, stewing in silence.

It is very commonly used with the prepositions over or about, and sometimes with in:

  • Stew over something → stewing over a bad decision
  • Stew about something → stewing about what he said
  • Stew in something → stewing in guilt / stewing in anger
The Connection Between the Two Meanings

The figurative meaning is actually a beautiful extension of the literal one. When you stew food, it sits in hot liquid, slowly, doing nothing but absorbing heat. When a person stews, they sit in their own emotional heat — worry, anger, guilt — slowly, doing nothing but absorbing it. The word is used as a metaphor because the experience feels the same: slow, trapped, hot, and going nowhere.

These come up often enough that you should know them:

1. "Stew in your own juice" (also: "stew in your own juices")
This means to suffer the consequences of your own actions, especially without anyone helping you or feeling sorry for you. It implies the person created the problem themselves and now has to sit in it.

  • He lied to everyone, so now he can stew in his own juice.
  • I'm not rescuing her — she made this mess; let her stew in her own juices.

2. "Let someone stew"
To deliberately leave someone in a state of worry, uncertainty, or discomfort — often as a form of punishment or to teach them a lesson. You know they are worried, but you choose not to relieve that worry.

  • He texted her five times with no reply. She was letting him stew.
  • After what he did, I decided to let him stew for a while before I called back.

• Stewing (in the figurative sense) is almost always passive. The person is not doing anything — they are just sitting with the feeling. This is why it often carries a slight negative tone: it suggests the person should do something but isn't.
  • The word implies duration. You don't stew for five minutes. You stew for hours, days, or longer.
  • It can describe both worry (fear-based) and simmering anger (resentment-based). Context usually makes clear which one it is.
  • When used in cooking, it can be transitive (you stew something: She stewed the lamb). When used figuratively about a person, it is usually intransitive (the person just stews: He stewed all day), though it can be transitive with the phrase "stew in" (stewing in regret).

SenseWhat it meansKey feeling

In cooking: stew means to cook food slowly in liquid over low heat for a long time.

In emotion: stew means to worry, brood, or feel upset about something quietly and for a long time, without taking action.

Both carry the same soul: something sitting in heat, slowly, going nowhere — until something changes.
15194:
A steward is a person who is trusted to look after, manage, or take care of something — not for themselves, but on behalf of others, or for the benefit of a larger group.

Think of it this way: imagine someone hands you the keys to their house and says, "I'm away for a year. Please take care of everything." In that moment, you become a steward. You didn't build the house. You don't own it. But you are now responsible for it. That sense of trust + responsibility + care on behalf of others is the soul of the word "steward."
The Different Faces of a Steward

The word is used in several real-world contexts, but the core idea stays the same across all of them.

1. A Person Who Manages Property or an Estate

Historically, wealthy landowners would hire a steward to run their entire estate — managing the land, the finances, the workers, and the day-to-day affairs — while the owner focused on other things or was away entirely. The steward was essentially the boss of the household, but always acting in the owner's interest, not his own.

"The steward oversaw every acre of the estate and reported directly to the lord."

2. A Person Who Serves Passengers on a Ship or Aircraft

On a ship or airplane, a steward is a person who looks after the comfort and needs of the passengers — serving food and drinks, answering questions, and ensuring everyone is safe and cared for during the journey.

On aircraft, you may be more familiar with the term "flight attendant" today, but "steward" (for men) and "stewardess" (for women) were the original terms for the same role.

"The steward brought warm blankets to the passengers as the ship sailed through the cold night."

3. A Shop Steward (in the Workplace)

In a workplace where workers belong to a union, a shop steward is a worker chosen by their fellow workers to represent them. This person speaks on behalf of the group in discussions with management — handling complaints, negotiating conditions, and making sure workers' rights are respected.

The steward here isn't a boss. They are a servant of their fellow workers — someone trusted to look after the group's interests.

"When the workers felt the new schedule was unfair, they brought the issue to their shop steward."

4. An Event Steward

At large events like sports matches, concerts, or public gatherings, stewards are the people in bright vests who guide crowds, maintain order, direct people to their seats, and respond to emergencies. They are responsible for the safety and smooth running of the event.

"The stewards directed thousands of fans safely into the stadium before the match began."

5. A Steward of the Environment (or any shared resource)

In a broader, more figurative sense, anyone who takes responsibility for protecting something that belongs to everyone — like nature, public land, a community, or even a tradition — can be called a steward of it.

"Farmers who protect the soil for future generations are true stewards of the land."
"As president of the club, she saw herself as a steward of its values and legacy."
The Single Thread Running Through All Meanings

No matter the context, a steward always has three things:

Responsibility — they are in charge of something.
Trust — someone (or a group, or society) has placed faith in them to handle it well.
Service to others — they are not managing for their own benefit, but for the benefit of someone else, a group, or the future.

A steward is never just a passive caretaker who does the bare minimum. The word carries a dignified weight — it implies that the person takes their responsibility seriously and acts with integrity.

You will almost certainly encounter the noun stewardship, which simply means the work, duty, or role of being a steward — the act of managing something responsibly on behalf of others.

"Under her stewardship, the company grew without losing its values."
"Good stewardship of public funds means spending them wisely and honestly."

Stewardship is the concept; a steward is the person who practices it.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see the word steward, ask yourself: "Who is taking care of what, on whose behalf?"

Answer that, and you've understood it perfectly.
15195:
Stewardship is the responsible management, care, and protection of something that has been entrusted to you — not as an owner, but as a caretaker — on behalf of others or for the benefit of future generations.

The single most important thing to understand about stewardship is this: the steward is not the owner. Someone (or something) has placed a valuable resource, asset, or responsibility in your hands, and you are expected to look after it wisely, preserve it, and ideally leave it in better shape than you found it.

Imagine your elderly grandparent owns a beautiful piece of farmland that has been in your family for generations. Before they pass away, they hand you the responsibility of managing it. You didn't create it. You don't own it in the deepest sense — it belongs to the family lineage, including the children and grandchildren who haven't been born yet. But now it's in your care.

Your job is to:

  • Farm it wisely, without exhausting the soil
  • Protect it from damage or neglect
  • Make thoughtful decisions about it
  • Eventually pass it on in good — or better — condition

That is stewardship.
What Sets Stewardship Apart from Simple Ownership

An owner can do whatever they want with what they own. They can spend it, sell it, neglect it, or even destroy it.

A steward cannot. A steward is bound by a duty. Their choices must serve the interest of whoever entrusted them, or the interest of the greater good. This creates a very specific moral and practical weight: you are responsible, but you are not free to be selfish.

This is why stewardship implies accountability. You answer to someone — shareholders, a community, future generations, God, society, or your own conscience — for how well you handled what was given to you.
The Key Elements Baked Into the Word

When someone uses the word "stewardship," all of these ideas are wrapped inside it:

  • Trust — Someone has trusted you enough to place something in your care
  • Responsibility — You are expected to manage it carefully; neglect is a failure
  • Active care — Stewardship isn't passive holding; it requires attention, effort, and good judgment
  • Long-term thinking — A good steward doesn't just think about today; they think about decades from now
  • Accountability — You must be able to answer for your decisions; you are not answerable only to yourself
Where You'll See This Word Used

Stewardship appears across many different areas of life. The meaning stays the same — only the subject changes.

Environmental stewardship refers to how humans manage the natural world: land, water, forests, air, and wildlife. A person or organization practicing environmental stewardship takes care of natural resources not just for today's use, but so that they survive for future generations. Governments, farmers, and conservation groups all talk about stewardship of the earth.

Financial stewardship refers to managing money responsibly on behalf of others. A nonprofit organization, for example, receives donations from the public. The people running it are stewards of that money — they don't own it personally; they must use it for the intended purpose and be transparent about where it goes. A CEO managing a company's finances is also exercising stewardship over the shareholders' assets.

Religious stewardship is a deeply rooted concept in many faiths, particularly Christianity, Islam, and Judaism. The idea is that the earth and its resources were created by God and belong to God. Humans are stewards — managers placed in charge of creation, expected to care for it wisely and humbly, not exploit it greedily.

Cultural stewardship refers to preserving traditions, art, language, and heritage for future generations. Museums, libraries, governments, and communities can all be stewards of cultural heritage.

Data stewardship, a more modern use, refers to the responsible handling of data — especially personal or sensitive data — ensuring it is accurate, secure, and used ethically.

Personal stewardship refers to managing your own resources — your time, your health, your talents, your relationships, your money — in a disciplined and responsible way, recognizing that what you have is ultimately not just yours to waste.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Stewardship is a word with weight and dignity. It carries a positive, even noble connotation. To call someone a good steward is a high compliment — it suggests they are trustworthy, wise, disciplined, and selfless. To accuse someone of poor stewardship is to say they failed a duty, wasted what they were given, or acted with short-sighted selfishness.

You will often hear phrases like:

  • "good stewardship of resources"
  • "environmental stewardship"
  • "stewardship of the land"
  • "a stewardship program"
  • "stewardship of public funds"
  • "practicing stewardship"

The word is especially common in formal, professional, governmental, religious, and environmental contexts. You're less likely to hear it in casual everyday conversation, but when you do hear it, it signals that something valuable is being managed on behalf of others — and that the speaker takes that responsibility seriously.

Understanding what stewardship isn't can sharpen the meaning.

The opposite of good stewardship is exploitation, negligence, or mismanagement. A company that strips a forest of all its trees with no replanting is failing in environmental stewardship. A treasurer who embezzles charity donations is failing in financial stewardship. A leader who runs an institution into the ground for personal gain is failing in organizational stewardship.

In each case, someone who was trusted to care for something instead took from it or damaged it.

If you had to distill stewardship to its essence: it is the responsible care and management of something valuable that belongs to others or to the future, carried out with integrity, accountability, and long-term thinking.
15196:
Before diving into specific meanings, here is a simple idea that runs through almost every use of "stick" as a verb:

Stick = something becoming fixed, attached, or held in one place — either by force, by choice, or by circumstance.

Once you feel this central idea, the many meanings of "stick" will make perfect sense.

1. To attach one thing to another using a sticky substance

This is the most basic, physical meaning. When something "sticks," it fastens itself to a surface because of glue, paste, tape, or its own natural stickiness.

"Stick the stamp on the envelope before mailing it."
"The chewing gum stuck to the bottom of her shoe."
"The wet leaves stuck to my jacket."

Notice the idea of two things becoming joined. One thing clings to another and doesn't come off easily.

2. To push a pointed object into something

Here, "stick" means to poke, jab, or insert a sharp or pointed object into something — to pierce or penetrate a surface.

"She stuck a needle into the fabric to sew it."
"He accidentally stuck himself with a pin."
"Stick a fork into the potato to check if it's cooked."
"The soldiers stuck their flags into the ground."

Think of it as making something enter by force at a sharp point.

3. To put or place something somewhere (informal)

In everyday spoken English, "stick" is used informally to mean simply "to put" something somewhere — usually quickly, casually, or without much care.

"Just stick the bags in the corner for now."
"She stuck her hand up to ask a question."
"Stick your name at the top of the page."
"He stuck his head through the window to look outside."

The tone here is relaxed and informal. You wouldn't use it in a formal essay, but you'll hear it constantly in conversation.

4. To be or become impossible (or very hard) to move

When something gets stuck, it is jammed, trapped, or held in one position and cannot move freely. This happens because of friction, blockage, or some obstacle. Notice that in this meaning, "stick" often appears in a past tense phrase: "got stuck" or "is stuck."

"The door is stuck — I can't open it."
"The drawer keeps sticking because the wood has swollen."
"The car got stuck in the mud."
"My zipper stuck halfway."

The idea: something that should move freely cannot, because something is holding or jamming it.

5. To remain, to last, to become permanent

This is a very important figurative meaning. When something "sticks," it stays. It doesn't go away. It becomes lasting or accepted. This applies to names, habits, rules, ideas, memories — anything that could either fade away or become permanent.

"They gave him the nickname 'Lucky,' and it stuck." (The nickname lasted. Everyone kept using it.)
"Some lessons from childhood really stick with you." (They stay in your memory for life.)
"The new policy was introduced, but it didn't stick." (People stopped following it; it didn't become permanent.)
"If you repeat something enough times, it sticks in your mind."

This is one of the most common uses of "stick" in everyday English. When something sticks, it doesn't disappear — it endures.

6. To stay in a place or situation (to not leave)

"Stick" can mean to remain somewhere — to not move away, to stay where you are, or to continue doing what you are doing. It carries a sense of persistence and loyalty.

"Stick close to me; this area is dangerous."
"He stuck in the same town his whole life."
"If you stick with the plan, things will work out."

7. To be unable to make progress (to be mentally blocked)

When you're working on something — a problem, a task, a question — and you cannot move forward, you are stuck. Your thinking is blocked.

"I'm totally stuck on question 4. I don't know how to solve it."
"She got stuck in the middle of her speech and forgot her lines."
"We were stuck on the same issue for days."

Again, this is the idea of being unable to move — but here it's mental rather than physical.

Phrasal verbs are combinations of "stick" with another small word (a preposition or adverb) that create a new, specific meaning. These are extremely common in English and are essential to know.

Stick to — to follow something closely and not deviate from it; to remain committed.

"Stick to the recipe exactly — don't experiment the first time."
"She stuck to her original answer even under pressure."
"If you stick to the main road, you won't get lost."

The idea: you are attached to something (a plan, a rule, a path) and you don't leave it.

Stick with — to continue doing something; to stay with a person, idea, or choice; to remain loyal.

"Learning a language is hard, but stick with it and you'll succeed."
"I'll stick with my current phone — it still works fine."
"His friends stuck with him during his difficult time."

Very similar to "stick to," but "stick with" often sounds warmer and more personal.

Stick out — has two related meanings:

(a) to protrude — to extend outward from a surface or place.

"His ears stick out a little."
"A piece of paper was sticking out from under the door."

(b) to be very noticeable; to be different from everything around you.

"With her bright red coat, she really stuck out in the crowd."
"His talent sticks out immediately — you notice it at once."

Stick up — has two distinct meanings:

(a) to point or extend upward.

"One corner of the poster is sticking up — press it down."
"His hair was sticking up in all directions after he woke up."

(b) (informal) to rob someone, usually with a weapon. (Less common in everyday conversation, but good to know.)

"The store was stuck up by two men wearing masks."

Stick up for — to defend someone (or yourself) when they are being attacked, criticized, or treated unfairly.

"Thank you for sticking up for me when everyone was criticizing my idea."
"You need to learn to stick up for yourself."

The image: you stand up (like raising a hand) in support of someone.

Stick around — to stay in a place and not leave, usually to wait for something.

"Stick around after the meeting — I need to talk to you."
"She stuck around for another hour in case someone needed her."

Stick together — to remain united as a group; to support each other and not separate.

"No matter what happens, our family sticks together."
"If we stick together, we can solve this problem."

Stick out for — to continue demanding something and refuse to accept less. (Used especially in negotiations or when someone is trying to get the best deal or outcome.)

"The workers stuck out for better pay and refused to settle for less."

Stick it out — to endure a difficult situation until it ends, without giving up.

"The first few months of training were brutal, but she stuck it out."
"He didn't enjoy his job, but he stuck it out until he found a better one."

These are fixed phrases where "stick" carries a figurative or idiomatic meaning. You'll hear them often.

"Stick to your guns" — to maintain your position, opinion, or decision firmly, even when others disagree or pressure you to change.

"Everyone told him to give up, but he stuck to his guns and eventually proved them wrong."

"Make it stick" — to make something effective, permanent, or accepted.

"The teacher tried several methods to make the grammar rule stick for her students."
"They signed the agreement, but it remained to be seen if the peace would stick."

"Stuck in a rut" — to be in a boring, repetitive situation where nothing changes and you feel unable to move forward.

"After doing the same job for fifteen years, he felt completely stuck in a rut."

"It stuck in my mind" — something remained in your memory very clearly. You couldn't forget it.

"That image from the film stuck in my mind for weeks."

"Stick in your throat" (also: "stick in your craw") — something that is very hard for you to accept, say, or swallow emotionally — it feels wrong or unacceptable.

"Having to apologize to someone she believed was wrong really stuck in her throat."

"Stick your neck out" — to take a risk on behalf of someone, or to express an opinion that might attract criticism or danger.

"He really stuck his neck out recommending her for the job — he hoped she wouldn't disappoint him."

"A sticking point" — a specific issue or detail in a discussion or negotiation that neither side can agree on; the thing that keeps blocking progress.

"Salary was the sticking point in the negotiation. Everything else had been agreed upon."

The best way to truly absorb "stick" is to notice how the same central idea — something becoming fixed or held in place — threads through every meaning:

  • Glue makes things physically fixed to each other → the sticker sticks
  • A needle forces its way into something → stick a pin in
  • Something jammed cannot move → the door is stuck
  • An idea that lasts won't leave your mind → it stuck with me
  • A loyal person won't leave someone's side → stick by a friend
  • Remaining committed means not drifting away from a plan → stick to the plan

Master this single idea — fixation, attachment, persistence — and you'll always have an intuition for what "stick" means, no matter how you encounter it.
15197:
A sticking point is a specific issue, topic, or problem that causes progress to stop or slow down significantly — something that people can't easily move past or agree on.

Think of it like a door with a sticky hinge. The door can swing most of the way, but it keeps getting stuck at one particular spot. That spot is the sticking point. Everything else moves fine — it's that one thing that keeps blocking the way forward.

The word "stick" here doesn't mean to glue something. It means to be stuck — unable to move. Just like a wheel stuck in mud, or a zipper stuck midway, a "sticking point" is the exact spot where movement stops.

Imagine you're pushing a heavy box across the floor. Most of the floor is smooth, and the box slides easily. But at one particular spot, there's a crack or a bump, and the box just won't go past it. That crack is the sticking point. Everything before it went fine. Everything after it would also go fine — if only you could get past that one point.

The term is extremely flexible and shows up across many areas of life:

1. Negotiations and Deals
This is the most common context. When two parties are trying to reach an agreement — whether it's a business deal, a salary negotiation, a peace treaty, or buying a car — they often agree on most things but get stuck on one specific issue. That issue is the sticking point.

"Both companies were happy with the partnership terms, but the division of profits was the sticking point."

"Salary was not the sticking point — the disagreement was over how many vacation days she'd get."

2. Learning and Education
A sticking point is a concept or skill that a student keeps struggling with — the exact spot where their understanding breaks down and they can't move forward.

"I understand most of calculus, but derivatives have always been my sticking point."

"For many people learning to drive, parallel parking is the biggest sticking point."

3. Projects and Problem-Solving
When a team is working on a project and keeps getting blocked at the same issue, that issue is the sticking point.

"Development on the app is mostly complete. The sticking point right now is getting security clearance from the compliance team."

4. Relationships and Conflicts
Two people may agree on almost everything but keep fighting about one thing — that one thing is their sticking point.

"They generally got along well. The sticking point in their friendship was always money — one was a spender, the other a saver."

5. Physical and Technical Contexts
In weightlifting, "sticking point" has a precise technical meaning: the position in a lift (like a squat or bench press) where the muscles are at their weakest mechanical advantage and the lifter is most likely to fail. It's the hardest point of the movement. Coaches specifically train people to strengthen their sticking point.

This physical meaning is probably the oldest use, and the figurative meanings grew from it.
Key Characteristics of a Sticking Point

Understanding these properties will help you recognize and use the term accurately:

It is specific, not general. A sticking point is never vague. It's not "things are going badly" — it's one particular, identifiable thing that is causing the blockage. You can point to it and name it.

It is persistent. A sticking point doesn't just slow things down once. It keeps coming up. It's a recurring bottleneck — every time you try to move forward, it stops you at the same place.

It blocks something that was otherwise progressing. A sticking point usually appears after things have been going smoothly. Everything else is fine — the sticking point is the exception, not the rule.

It may or may not be solvable. Sometimes sticking points get resolved through compromise, creativity, or one side giving in. Other times, they permanently block a deal or a process.
How a Sticking Point Gets Resolved

There are typically a few ways:

  • Compromise — Both sides give a little on that specific issue.
  • Concession — One party agrees to the other's terms on that issue.
  • Creative reframing — The issue gets reframed or restructured so it no longer causes a conflict (e.g., in a salary negotiation, instead of raising the base pay, the employer offers a larger bonus — this sidesteps the sticking point).
  • Dropping it — Sometimes both sides agree to skip the sticking point entirely and build around it.
  • It remains unresolved — And if no one can get past it, the negotiation fails, the project stalls, or the conflict continues.
How It's Different from Similar Words

These are easy to confuse, so here's the distinction:

Sticking point vs. Problem: A "problem" is broad. A sticking point is a specific problem that blocks progress at a particular moment. All sticking points are problems, but not all problems are sticking points.

Sticking point vs. Obstacle: An obstacle is something in your way. A sticking point is something that stops you at a specific spot. The image of an obstacle is something you walk toward and then trip over. The image of a sticking point is something you keep getting wedged at — you can get close, but can't get past.

Sticking point vs. Dealbreaker: A dealbreaker is absolute — it ends things entirely, no question. A sticking point is something you're trying to resolve — it's making things hard, but it may not be fatal. A dealbreaker has no negotiation left. A sticking point still has hope.

IdeaSimple Version
What it meansThe specific issue that keeps blocking progress
Where it's usedNegotiations, learning, projects, conflicts, physical training
What makes it uniqueIt is specific, persistent, and appears during otherwise smooth progress
How it's resolvedCompromise, concession, creativity, or sometimes it isn't
One Final Way to Remember It

Picture a screw that's almost all the way in. You've turned it 99% of the way without trouble. But then, right near the end, it just won't go any further — it's stuck. That's the sticking point. It's never at the very beginning. It's never a general all-over problem. It's always that one specific, maddening spot where everything stops — right when you were almost there.

That's exactly what "sticking point" means in every context you'll ever encounter it.
15198: A stickler is a person who insists — very strongly and very strictly — on something being done the right way, with no shortcuts, no exceptions, and no compromises. Whatever that "something" is, a stickler takes it extremely seriously and will not let even a small mistake or deviation slide.
The Key Pattern: "A Stickler For Something"

This word almost always appears in one pattern:

a stickler for [something]

The word for tells you what the person is strict about. You simply cannot call someone "a stickler" without (at least implying) what they are a stickler for. Here are clear examples:

  • A stickler for grammar → someone who insists that language must be written and spoken with perfect grammatical correctness. They will notice and point out every misplaced comma or wrong verb form.
  • A stickler for punctuality → someone who insists that people must arrive exactly on time — not a minute late. Being five minutes late is simply unacceptable to them.
  • A stickler for the rules → someone who insists that rules must be followed to the letter. They won't bend a rule even when it would be harmless and convenient to do so.
  • A stickler for detail → someone who pays extreme attention to even the smallest details and insists that nothing is overlooked or done carelessly.
  • A stickler for cleanliness → someone who insists that everything must be spotlessly clean. A small mess is a big problem to them.

Being a stickler is stronger than simply caring about something. Consider this scale:

  • "She cares about grammar." → normal, relaxed concern.
  • "She is particular about grammar." → more careful, more attentive.
  • "She is a stickler for grammar." → she insists on it, watches for it constantly, and will not tolerate errors. It almost defines her.

A stickler doesn't just prefer things a certain way — they demand it, even when others think it isn't worth the fuss.
The Tone: Is It Good or Bad?

The word "stickler" sits in an interesting middle ground — it is not purely negative or purely positive. Its tone depends entirely on the situation and the speaker's perspective.

It can sound negative when the stickler's strictness seems excessive, unnecessary, or annoying to others. For example:

"Our manager is a real stickler for formatting. He sent back my entire report because the margins were wrong by half an inch."

Here, the listener probably feels some sympathy for the writer, and the manager comes across as overly rigid.

It can sound neutral or even admiring when the strictness is seen as responsible, professional, or admirable. For example:

"The surgeon is a stickler for hygiene in the operating room — and that's exactly the kind of doctor you want."

Here, being a stickler sounds like a genuinely good quality.

So the word itself doesn't judge the person — it simply describes their strict, uncompromising nature. You decide from context whether that's reasonable or excessive.

If it helps, imagine a strict teacher who always carries a red pen. The moment they see a spelling mistake, they circle it. They never ignore errors "just this once." They hold everyone — including themselves — to a very high, very precise standard in whatever area they care about. That teacher is a stickler.

Or imagine a referee who calls every foul, no matter how small, and never looks the other way. A stickler never looks the other way.

It's worth clarifying what the word does not mean:

  • A stickler is not a bully or a cruel person — they are simply strict and exacting.
  • A stickler is not necessarily someone who is strict about everything — a person can be a stickler for just one thing (e.g., punctuality) and be relaxed about everything else.
  • A stickler is not someone who is merely organized or careful — the key is that they insist and enforce, often making others feel the pressure too.

A stickler is someone who absolutely insists on a particular standard being met — completely, precisely, and without exception. They refuse to let anything slide in the area they care about.

If you remember one thing: "a stickler for X" = someone who takes X incredibly seriously and will always push for it to be done perfectly.
15199: If someone says you are "on a sticky wicket", it means you are in a difficult, awkward, or tricky situation — one that is hard to handle and where any wrong move could make things worse.
Where It Comes From — The Cricket Origin

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand where it was born: the sport of cricket, which is hugely popular in Britain, India, Australia, Pakistan, and other Commonwealth countries.

First, what is a "wicket"?

In cricket, the word "wicket" has a couple of meanings, but for this idiom, it refers to the pitch — the long, flat strip of ground in the middle of the cricket field where the bowler bowls and the batsman bats. This strip of ground is the most important piece of real estate in the entire game.

Now, what makes a wicket "sticky"?

Imagine this: it rains heavily before a match or during a break in play. The pitch gets soaked with water. Then the sun comes out, and the pitch begins to dry.

Here is the problem: when a wet pitch starts drying out under the sun, it does not dry evenly. The surface becomes soft, damp, and unpredictable. The ball no longer bounces in a straight, reliable way. Instead, it might:

  • Suddenly shoot along the ground and stay low
  • Or rear up sharply and fly towards the batsman's face
  • Or grip the surface and turn in a direction the batsman did not expect

The batsman, standing with his bat, has no idea what the ball will do. He makes his best guess, plays his shot — and the ball does something completely different. It is, quite simply, an extremely difficult and treacherous situation to bat in.

The wet, drying pitch was literally sticky — the ball would grip and cling to the surface. So the term "sticky wicket" was born.

This is also sometimes called a "sticky dog" or a "glue pot" in old cricketing language, but those terms are now quite rare. "Sticky wicket" is the one that survived.
How the Cricket Meaning Became an Idiom

The leap from cricket to everyday language is very natural once you picture the batsman on that treacherous pitch:

  • He is in a situation not entirely of his own making (the rain fell, not because of him).
  • The conditions are working against him.
  • He must act carefully, because one wrong move means he is out.
  • No matter what he does, it is hard to come out well.

People saw this as a perfect image for any difficult situation in life — at work, in relationships, in politics — where you are in a tight spot, the conditions are against you, and you need to tread very carefully.
How to Use It — In Real Life

The most common way to use this idiom is the phrase "on a sticky wicket."

Here are clear, natural examples:

"The minister is on a sticky wicket after those leaked documents."

(He is in a difficult, uncomfortable position politically.)

"I was on a sticky wicket when my boss asked me why the project was delayed."

(I was in an awkward spot where I had to choose my words very carefully.)

"Asking her to work overtime again this week — that's a sticky wicket."

(That's a tricky, delicate situation.)

"He found himself on a sticky wicket trying to explain where the money had gone."

(He was in a hard-to-escape, difficult situation.)

Notice that the phrase is almost always used as "on a sticky wicket" — as if the person is literally standing on that wet, unreliable pitch.
The Exact Shade of Meaning — What Makes It Special

This idiom is not just about any difficulty. It carries a specific flavour:

  1. Unpredictability — The situation is tricky partly because you cannot be sure what will happen next, just like the batsman who doesn't know how the ball will bounce.
  2. Delicacy — You have to act carefully. A blunt or clumsy response will make things worse.
  3. No easy exit — There is no clean, simple way out. You have to navigate carefully.
  4. Often not fully your fault — Like the rain wetting the pitch, the awkward situation may have arisen from circumstances outside your control.

So it is slightly stronger and more specific than just saying "a difficult situation." It suggests a situation that is both tricky AND fragile, where your own handling of it really matters.

This is primarily British English. You will hear it most often in:

  • Britain, Australia, India, New Zealand, South Africa, and other cricket-playing nations
  • Formal and semi-formal contexts — newspapers, political commentary, business discussions, polite conversation
  • It has a slightly old-fashioned, educated feel to it — it is not street slang, but it is not stiff or cold either. It is the kind of phrase a journalist, a politician, a professor, or your well-read uncle might use.

Americans generally do not use this phrase, since cricket is not part of their culture. If you use it in conversation with an American, they may not understand it straight away.
Similar Idioms — The Same Family of Meaning

If you want to express the same idea in other ways, here are some related English idioms:

  • "In a tight spot" — in a difficult situation
  • "In a pickle" — in a tricky, awkward situation (more informal, light-hearted)
  • "Between a rock and a hard place" — forced to choose between two bad options
  • "In hot water" — in trouble, especially trouble caused by your own actions
  • "Walking on thin ice" — in a risky situation where one wrong move causes disaster

Among these, "sticky wicket" is the most refined and the most specific about the idea of unpredictability and the need for careful handling.

Whenever you hear "sticky wicket," picture a batsman standing helplessly on a wet, drying cricket pitch, watching the ball bounce in impossible, random directions, completely unsure what to do next.

That image is the idiom.
"Sticky wicket" = a difficult, tricky, delicate situation that is hard to get out of cleanly, where you must act carefully because conditions are unpredictable and working against you.
